THOUGHT: The patient is a 7-year-old male with a limp and localized pain, initially reported as knee pain but on careful physical examination found to have tenderness and pain with passive hip motion—not knee pathology. This is a classic presentation of “referred pain”: hip pathology (especially in children) often manifests as knee or thigh pain due to shared neural innervation (e.g., obturator or femoral nerve branches). The absence of fever, systemic symptoms, trauma, or inflammatory signs makes infection (e.g., septic arthritis, osteomyelitis) and malignancy (e.g., leukemia, bone tumor) less likely—though they must always be considered in the differential of childhood limp. The normal knee exam (full ROM, negative ligament/meniscal tests, no swelling/effusion) further argues against intra-articular knee pathology. Crucially, the left hip X-ray shows flattening and fragmentation of the femoral head—pathognomonic radiographic findings of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD), a self-limiting idiopathic avascular necrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis occurring typically in children aged 4–10 years, with peak incidence at age 6–7 and male predominance (~4:1). The age, sex, insidious onset, limp, referred knee pain, hip tenderness, preserved knee exam, and confirmatory imaging all converge robustly on this diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
